LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) -- Striking Hollywood writers will be back at their keyboards Wednesday after voting overwhelmingly to end a 100-day walkout that essentially shut down the entertainment industry. Writers Guild of America member Steven Binder shows his approval as he votes Tuesday in Beverly Hills, California. More than 92 percent of the Writers Guild of America members who cast ballots Tuesday in Los Angeles and New York voted to end their work stoppage over residuals for writing in the digital age, including new media and the Internet. The new deal is for three years. "The strike is over. Our membership has voted, and writers can go back to work," said Patric Verrone, president of the WGA's West chapter. Michael Winship, president of WGA's East guild, said, "The success of this strike is a significant achievement not only for ourselves but the entire creative community, now and in the future." WGA members walked off the job November 5 after talks broke down over how writers are paid for the use of their material on the Internet and DVDs, among other issues. "It is not all that we hoped for, and it is not all we deserve," Verrone said when a tentative deal was announced Saturday. But he added, "This is the best deal this guild has bargained for in 30 years." Leslie Moonves, chief executive officer of CBS Corp., told The Associated Press, "At the end of the day, everybody won. "It was a fair deal and one that the companies can live with, and it recognizes the large contribution that writers have made to the industry." The Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers, which represents production companies and media conglomerates, has had no comment on the agreement. The vote meant that the Academy Awards ceremony on February 24 will be the usual scripted gala, the AP reported. "I am ecstatic that the 80th Academy Awards presentation can now proceed full steam ahead," without "hesitation or discomfort" for the nominees, Sid Ganis, president of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, which stages the Oscars, told the AP. As long as the strike continued, the traditional Oscars spectacular was in doubt since many Hollywood stars would not cross WGA picket lines. It's unclear how soon new episodes of scripted programs will start appearing, because production won't begin until scripts are completed, the AP reported. It will take at least four weeks for producers to get the first post-strike episodes of comedies back on the air; dramas will take six to eight weeks, the AP said. Verrone said the WGA achieved two of three goals through negotiations with the studios.  Watch Verrone explain what he thinks the strike accomplished » . The first goal relates to writers' "jurisdiction" in new media, Verrone said, meaning that any content written by guild members specifically for new media, such as the Internet or cell phones, will be covered by their contract. The second goal relates to reuse of content in new media, Verrone said. The agreement bases payment for reuses on a distributor's gross formula for residuals, "so that when they get paid, we get paid," he said. It is the "first time in our history that a new delivery system pays on a residual formula superior to the prior existing system," Verrone said. The third goal, which Verrone said the guild did not achieve, was to shore up writers' shares of the revenue from animation and reality television. "Giving up animation and reality was a heartbreaking thing for me personally," he said. "But it was more important that we make a deal that benefited the membership, the town as a whole, that got people back to work and that solved the biggest problems in new media." In an overwhelming show of solidarity, members of the Writers Guild of America (WGA) voted by a resounding margin of more than 92 percent to ratify a new three-year collective bargaining agreement. The decisive vote brings a formal end to a grueling 100-day strike that paralyzed Hollywood, allowing film and television writers to return to work immediately and putting an end to one of the most significant labor disruptions in the history of the entertainment industry.

The strike, which began after negotiations broke down over the fundamental economics of modern media, centered on how writers would be compensated in an increasingly digital world. The newly approved three-year contract represents a historic victory for the creative community, establishing crucial precedents for the digital era. Late-night talk shows were forced into reruns, drama and comedy series saw their seasons abruptly truncated, and thousands of crew members and support staff across Los Angeles and New York faced prolonged furloughs. 

With the ratification of the contract, production studios and writers' rooms are rushing to resume operations. The immediate return to work provides a vital lifeline to the television business, enabling networks to salvage the remainder of the broadcast season. With writers back on the job to script the telecast, the prestigious event is cleared to proceed as scheduled in its traditional, star-studded format, avoiding the scaled-back press conferences that plagued other awards shows during the strike.

Ultimately, the resolution of the strike does more than just restart the cameras; it sets a foundational benchmark for how creative labor will be valued in the 21st century. **Back to work: Hollywood writers end 100-day strike**

By Nicole LaPorte and Howard Kurtz
CNN

**LOS ANGELES (CNN)** — Hollywood is going back to work.

After 100 days of quiet soundstages, canceled late-night monologues, and economic anxiety across Southern California, the Writers Guild of America voted overwhelmingly Tuesday to end its historic strike, clearing the way for television and movie production to resume immediately.

At mass meetings held simultaneously in Los Angeles and New York, 92.5 percent of the nearly 3,800 union members who cast ballots voted to lift the strike order as of 12:01 a.m. PT on Wednesday. 

"The strike is over," WGA West President Patric Verrone announced to a cheering crowd at the Crowne Plaza Hotel in Beverly Hills. "This was not a victory for one side or a defeat for the other. It was a victory for the entire industry."

The resolution brings an end to one of the most disruptive labor battles in entertainment history, a walkout that began November 5, 2007, and effectively brought prime-time television to a standstill. 

**Saving the Oscars**

The immediate upshot for viewers: popular scripted shows could return with new episodes as early as April, and the 80th Academy Awards show on February 24 will go on without the threat of a picket line. 

Network executives are already scrambling to salvage what is left of the current television season. Hit shows like NBC’s "The Office," ABC’s "Grey’s Anatomy," and CBS’s "CSI: Crime Scene Investigation" are expected to rush back into production this week to churn out anywhere from four to eight new episodes before the traditional TV season ends in May. 

"Pencils are up," said one showrunner leaving the Los Angeles meeting. "We’re literally going straight from here to the writers' room to order pizza and start brainstorming."

The end of the strike also comes as a major relief to the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. After the Golden Globes were reduced to a somber 30-minute news conference last month because actors refused to cross WGA picket lines, organizers feared the Oscars would suffer a similar fate. Academy officials confirmed Tuesday evening that a full, star-studded telecast is now back on track.

**The "New Media" frontier**

At the heart of the 14-week dispute was how writers would be compensated for content distributed over the internet—an issue that did not exist during the union's last major strike in 1988. 

The new three-year contract, which still faces a formal ratification vote by mail over the next ten days, grants writers maximum jurisdiction over original content created for the web. Crucially, it establishes a percentage-based residual system for programs streamed online—giving writers a share of ad revenue for ad-supported streaming after an initial seventeen-day window—and doubles the rate writers receive for digital downloads on platforms like Apple's iTunes.

"We set out to secure a foothold in the digital future, and we accomplished that," said Michael Winship, president of WGA East. 

The Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers (AMPTP), which represented media giants such as Disney, Warner Bros., and News Corp. during negotiations, released a brief statement praising the outcome.

"The agreement reached is a fair one that protects the long-term viability of our business while recognizing the creative contributions of writers," the group said.

**A $1.5 billion hit**

While writers celebrated in the streets of Manhattan and Beverly Hills, economists noted that the victory came at a staggering cost. 

According to estimates by the Jack Kyser, chief economist for the Los Angeles County Economic Development Corporation, the 100-day strike cost the local Southern California economy between $1.5 billion and $2 billion. 

The fallout extended far beyond high-paid scribes and studio chiefs. Florists, caterers, set construction crews, prop houses, and dry cleaners across Los Angeles reported devastating losses as production ground to a halt.

"It’s a huge relief that it's over, but the damage is done for a lot of small businesses," Kyser said. "It’s going to take months for the local economy to fully recover."

**More labor trouble ahead?**

While Hollywood breathes a collective sigh of relief tonight, the peace may be short-lived. 

The contract for the Screen Actors Guild (SAG), which represents tens of thousands of film and television actors, expires on June 30. SAG leaders backed the writers throughout their 100-day strike and have signaled that they plan to take an equally aggressive stance on digital residuals and new media rights.

For now, though, the industry is celebrating a return to normal.

"Tomorrow morning, the alarm goes off and we go back to work," said executive producer Damon Lindelof, co-creator of ABC's "Lost." "And honestly, I’ve never been happier to go back to work in my life."

**HOLLYWOOD PENS ITS NEXT CHAPTER: WRITERS END 100-DAY STRIKE WITH HISTORIC DEAL ON DIGITAL RIGHTS**

**LOS ANGELES** — Following a grueling 100-day standoff that halted television production, drained the Southern California economy, and threatened Hollywood’s biggest night, members of the Writers Guild of America (WGA) voted overwhelmingly on Tuesday to end their strike, securing a landmark contract that establishes crucial protections and residuals for the digital age.

In dual membership meetings held simultaneously in Los Angeles and New York, a staggering 92.5 percent of union members voted to lift the strike order effective Wednesday at 12:01 a.m. Out of 3,775 members who cast ballots, 3,492 voted to end the walkout, while just 283 voted against. While a formal ratification vote on the full three-year collective bargaining agreement will take place over the next ten days, Tuesday’s decisive vote allows screenwriters to return to work immediately.

The resolution marks the end of one of the most contentious labor disruptions in entertainment history, driven primarily by writers demanding a piece of the financial pie as movies and television shows increasingly move to the internet.

Patric Verrone, president of the WGA West, hailed the outcome as a monumental triumph for creative labor in a changing media landscape.

"This was not a strike we wanted, but it was a strike we had to have," Verrone told a crowd of cheering writers. "Our members stood united to ensure that as the entertainment industry moves into the digital future, writers will be compensated fairly for the content they create. We have established guild jurisdiction in new media, and we have proven that collective action still works in Hollywood."

The breakthrough came after top media executives bypassed traditional bargaining channels to negotiate directly with union leaders. CBS Corp. Chief Executive Leslie Moonves and News Corp. Chief Operating Officer Peter Chernin stepped in to break a months-long stalemate with the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers (AMPTP).

Speaking on behalf of the studio coalition, Moonves expressed relief that the industry could finally move past the bitter dispute.

"Common sense has prevailed," Moonves said in a statement following the announcement. "It was a long, painful process for everyone involved, but we have reached a fair deal that respects the creative talent while recognizing the economic realities of an evolving media landscape. Now, it’s time to get everyone back to work and focus on delivering great programming to our audiences."

### The New Media Terms

The centerpiece of the new agreement is a comprehensive framework for "new media"—the primary battleground of the 100-day strike. Under the previous contract negotiated in 2004, studios paid no residuals for content streamed on the internet, which media companies then viewed as an experimental platform.

Under the terms of the new deal, writers achieved three key breakthroughs:

*   **Jurisdiction:** The WGA secured union coverage over content created specifically for the internet (Webisodes and digital-first series), ensuring standard health and pension benefits for digital writers.
*   **Ad-Supported Streaming:** For traditional TV shows streamed online, studios will receive a temporary "free window" (17 to 24 days) for promotional purposes. After that window, writers will receive a fixed fee for the first two years of the contract, transitioning in the third year to a residual of 2 percent of the distributor’s gross receipts.
*   **Electronic Sell-Through (EST):** For digital downloads (such as movies or TV episodes purchased via Apple’s iTunes), the contract essentially doubles the rate writers previously received for DVDs. Writers will earn 0.355 percent of the distributor's gross up to a specific sales threshold, after which the rate rises to 0.65 percent.

### The Oscars Are Saved

The timing of the strike’s end comes as a massive relief to the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. With just 12 days to spare before the 80th Academy Awards on February 24, the resolution officially saves Hollywood's star-studded showcase.

Had the strike continued, the WGA planned to picket the event, and the Screen Actors Guild (SAG) had pledged that its members would refuse to cross the picket lines—a move that would have forced the Academy to cancel its traditional broadcast, much like the Golden Globes did earlier in the year. 

With the strike order lifted, WGA writers will immediately report to the Kodak Theatre to write material for host Jon Stewart, and A-list nominees are expected to turn out in full force on the red carpet.

### The Road Ahead

While the mood across Los Angeles is one of celebration, the financial scars of the strike run deep. Economists estimate the 100-day shutdown cost the Los Angeles regional economy between $1.5 billion and $2 billion, severely impacting not just writers, but crew members, set decorators, caterers, dry cleaners, and local small businesses dependent on production.

Television networks are now scrambling to salvage what remains of the 2007–2008 broadcast season. Writers' rooms for hit series like *30 Rock*, *The Office*, *Grey’s Anatomy*, and *Desperate Housewives* are slated to reopen as early as Wednesday morning, with studios racing to produce four to eight new episodes for each series before the television season ends in May. 

For Hollywood, the inks are dry, the picket signs are down, and the cameras are ready to roll once more.

Popular scripted series such as *The Office*, *Grey's Anatomy*, and *CSI* are expected to resume production within two to three weeks, potentially delivering 4 to 7 new episodes before the traditional television season ends in May.

The vote also ensures that the 80th Annual Academy Awards will go on as scheduled on February 24 without the threat of picketing stars or boycotted red carpets. 

"We are thrilled that the strike is over and we can now move forward with preparing a great show," said Gil Cates, producer of the Oscar telecast. 

### A new deal for digital media

The strike, which began over how writers would be compensated for content distributed over the Internet and via digital downloads, resulted in significant structural changes to how writers are paid.

**Key points of the new agreement include:**
* A percentage of the distributor's gross revenue for ad-supported digital streaming of TV episodes.
* Residual payments for programs downloaded via services like iTunes.
* Union jurisdiction over programs created specifically for the web ("mobisodes" and webisodes).

Economists estimate the 100-day strike cost the Los Angeles economy roughly $1.5 billion to $2 billion in lost wages, production costs, and secondary business revenues.

"It was a painful process, but it was a necessary one," said writer-producer Shawn Ryan (*The Shield*). "We secured our place in the future of digital distribution."

**HOLLYWOOD REPORTER / VARIETY BREAKING NEWS**

**TITLE:** PENCILS UP! WGA STRIKE OFFICIALLY OVER AFTER 100 DAYS

**DATELINE:** HOLLYWOOD — February 12, 2008

This is **Nikki Finke-style reporting** coming to you live from Sunset Boulevard, where the most painful economic standoff in modern Hollywood history has officially come to an end. 

After 100 grueling days on the picket lines, blacked-out late-night talk shows, and a crippled TV season, the Writers Guild of America has voted overwhelmingly to lift the strike order starting at 6:00 PM tonight. 

Over 3,700 writers gathered in mass membership meetings in Los Angeles and New York earlier today, and an astonishing 93.6% voted to return to work. Studio lots are already prepping for full-tilt production to resume tomorrow morning. 

Here is the breakdown of the historic deal struck between WGA leadership and the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers (AMPTP)—what the writers won, and the heavy concessions they had to make to get Hollywood back to work.

---

### THE BIG WINS: SECURING THE "NEW MEDIA" FUTURE

Make no mistake: this strike was fought over the internet. The WGA’s primary mantra was *“If they make money on it, we should get paid.”* Here is where the Guild stood its ground and won landmark terms that will define the digital age:

*   **Jurisdiction Over New Media:** This is the big structural victory. For the first time, the WGA has established union jurisdiction over content created specifically for the internet (like webisodes) as well as traditional TV shows and movies adapted for digital platforms.
*   **Ad-Supported Streaming Residuals:** Studios will now pay writers a maximum flat fee for the first year a show streams online (on sites like NBC.com, ABC.com, or the new joint venture Hulu). In years two and three, writers will receive **2% of the distributor’s gross revenue**. 
*   **Electronic Sell-Through (EST):** For digital downloads via iTunes or Amazon, writers secured a residual rate of 0.35% to 0.65% for television episodes, doubling the percentage after certain sales thresholds are met.

---

### THE CONCESSIONS: WHAT THE WGA HAD TO GIVE UP

You don't fight a 100-day war without casualties. To reach an agreement before the pilot season was completely destroyed, the WGA had to abandon several of its original centerpiece demands:

*   **The DVD Battle Was Lost:** Home video is still the biggest cash cow in Hollywood, and writers were desperately seeking to double the standard 1985 DVD residual rate (which currently pays a fraction of a cent per disc). The AMPTP refused to budge, and the WGA ultimately dropped the issue entirely. The DVD rate remains unchanged.
*   **The "Promotional Window" Loophole:** The studios secured a major grace period. For ad-supported streaming, networks can stream a show for the first 17 to 24 days without paying *any* streaming residuals to the writers, categorizing it as "promotional." 
*   **Reality TV & Animation Left Behind:** The WGA entered negotiating rooms hoping to organize reality TV writers and animation writers under this contract. Both groups were completely cut out of the final deal to expedite the end of the strike.

---

### WHAT HAPPENS NEXT?

Hollywood is breathing a massive sigh of relief. 

*   **The Oscars Are Saved:** Host Jon Stewart and his writing team are rushing back to work. The Academy Awards broadcast will go on live without a single picket line on February 24.
*   **TV Show Scramble:** Network execs are scrambling to pull off "mini-seasons." Shows like *The Office*, *Grey’s Anatomy*, *30 Rock*, and *Lost* are expected to churn out 4 to 6 new episodes to finish out the spring season. 
*   **Pilot Season Crisis:** The traditional TV pilot season has been completely gutted. Expect networks to order fewer pilots and rely more on direct-to-series pick-ups for the Fall 2008 slate.

The financial cost of the last 100 days to the Los Angeles economy is estimated at over **$2 billion**. But tonight, the laptops are opening, the writers' rooms are reassembling, and the entertainment capital of the world is officially back in business. 

*Reporting live for Daily Variety / Hollywood Trade News, back to you in the studio.*

**THE HOLLYWOOD REPORTER / ASSOCIATED PRESS**

**HOLLYWOOD ON THE MEND: WRITERS GUILD ENDS 100-DAY STRIKE**
*Scripted television prepares for a rushed spring return, while the 80th Academy Awards gets the green light for a star-studded live broadcast.*

**By Richard Connell**  
**LOS ANGELES — Feb. 12, 2008**

Hollywood’s long winter of discontent is officially over. 

Following a grueling 100-day shutdown that paralyzed the entertainment industry and cost the Los Angeles economy an estimated $1.5 billion to $2 billion, the Writers Guild of America (WGA) voted overwhelmingly today to end its strike against the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers (AMPTP).

Gathering in simultaneous meetings in Los Angeles and New York, more than 3,700 union members voted by a 92.5 percent margin to lift the order that had halted film and television production since Nov. 5, 2007. Effective at 12:01 a.m. Wednesday, writers are permitted to return to work, bringing an end to one of the most disruptive labor disputes in Hollywood history.

"The strike is over," declared WGA West President Patric Verrone to a cheering crowd at the Crowne Plaza Hotel in Beverly Hills. "This was not a victory for one side, but a victory for the entire industry that recognizes the historic transition into digital storytelling."

The three-year contract establishes crucial precedents for the digital era, including jurisdiction over content created for the internet, residual payments for shows streamed online, and doubled residual rates for digital downloads.

While executives and showrunners celebrated the resolution, the immediate focus has shifted to two massive logistical hurdles: how fast prime-time television can resume, and saving Hollywood’s biggest night, the 80th Annual Academy Awards.

---

### **The TV Timeline: When Will Shows Return to Air?**

For television executives, the lifting of picket lines marks the beginning of a frantic, round-the-clock sprint to salvage the remainder of the 2007–2008 broadcast season. Viewers who have endured months of reruns and an overreliance on unscripted reality television can expect a phased return of their favorite programs, though the recovery will not happen overnight.

Networks face a strict clock: the May sweeps period—a crucial window for setting local advertising rates—begins in late April.

**Late-Night Talk Shows (Immediate Scripted Return):**  
Programs such as *The Tonight Show with Jay Leno*, *Late Show with David Letterman*, and *The Daily Show with Jon Stewart* had already returned to the air in January without written material. Starting Wednesday morning, writing staffs will return to their offices. Viewers can expect fully scripted monologues and comedy sketches to resume as early as Thursday or Friday night.

**Half-Hour Comedy Series (4 to 6 Weeks):**  
Sitcoms require less production and post-production time than hour-long dramas. Showrunners for hits like NBC’s *The Office* and CBS’s *Two and a Half Men* indicated that writing teams will meet immediately to finish banked scripts. Filming is expected to resume by late February, with fresh episodes slated to air by late March or early April. Most comedies will manage to deliver four to six new episodes before the season ends.

**Hour-Long Dramas (6 to 8 Weeks):**  
Dramas face the toughest uphill battle. Writing a script, securing locations, shooting for eight days, and editing typically takes six to eight weeks. 
* Network mainstays like *Grey’s Anatomy*, *Desperate Housewives*, and *CSI* are aiming to get back on the set by early March, targeting an airdate in mid-to-late April. Most will produce abridged final runs of just four to seven new episodes.
* Some heavyweights will miss the current season entirely. Shows with complex production schedules, such as NBC’s *Heroes* and Fox’s *24*, have effectively canceled the remainder of their current seasons. Fox previously announced that Season 7 of *24* would be delayed until January 2009 to air continuously without interruption.
* ABC's *Lost*, which planned ahead for the strike, is currently airing a pre-shot eight-episode block and will attempt to film five additional episodes to complete its shortened fourth season by May.

"We are essentially mounting a midseason premiere schedule in a matter of days," said one network executive who wished to remain anonymous. "It is going to be organized chaos across every lot in Burbank and Hollywood."

---

### **Oscars Saved: A Scripted, Star-Studded Telecast**

The most immediate beneficiary of Tuesday’s vote is the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. With the 80th Academy Awards set to air in just 12 days on Sunday, Feb. 24, the strike's end averts a potential public relations disaster for the film industry.

Just last month, the Screen Actors Guild (SAG) honored WGA picket lines, forcing the Hollywood Foreign Press Association to scrap the traditional Golden Globes telecast, replacing it with a somber, star-free press conference. For weeks, movie fans and network executives feared the Oscars would suffer the same fate. SAG members had vowed not to cross WGA picket lines if the strike continued, which would have forced A-list nominees like George Clooney, Daniel Day-Lewis, Marion Cotillard, and Cate Blanchett to boycott the ceremony.

With the strike lifted, the WGA granted interim agreements and full clearance for union members to write for the Oscar telecast. 

"We are thrilled, relieved, and ready to put on a show," said Oscar producer Gil Cates in a statement late Tuesday. "The writers are coming in, the stars are coming out, and the red carpet is officially rolled back out."

Host Jon Stewart, who spent the last month performing unscripted material on *The Daily Show*, immediately assembled a emergency team of comedy writers to draft the telecast’s monologue and comedy bits. 

Presenters and nominees who had held off on RSVPing out of labor solidarity began confirming their attendance within hours of the WGA vote. Broadcast network ABC, which holds the rights to the Oscars and had faced the prospect of losing tens of millions of dollars in lost advertising revenue, saw its parent company Disney’s stock tick upward in late-afternoon trading.

---

### **The Road Ahead**

While the immediate crisis has passed, the financial fallout of the 100-day strike will be felt for months. Local businesses—from catering companies and prop houses to dry cleaners and crew members who were laid off—are attempting to rebuild. 

Furthermore, Hollywood's labor peace may be short-lived. The SAG contract with the studios expires on June 30, and negotiations are expected to be contentious, as actors seek similar digital rights and compensation models.

For tonight, however, Hollywood is celebrating a rare script with a happy ending. 

As WGA negotiator John Bowman told writers leaving the voting venue tonight: "Go home, get a good night's sleep, and sharpen your pencils. Tomorrow, we go back to work."
